title: Don Quixote
body: Cervantes published his novel in two parts, in 1605 and 1615. The story of a man who has read too many tales of chivalry and sets out as a knight is often called the first modern novel.

title: The Divine Comedy
body: Dante Alighieri wrote the poem in the early 14th century. It follows a journey through Hell, Purgatory and Paradise. Written in Tuscan rather than Latin, it did much to shape the Italian literary language.

title: Impressionism
body: The movement took its name from Claude Monet's painting Impression, Sunrise, shown at an exhibition in Paris in 1874; a critic used the word mockingly. The Impressionists painted light and passing moments with visible brushstrokes, often outdoors.

title: War and Peace
body: Leo Tolstoy's novel, published in full in 1869, follows Russian aristocratic families through Napoleon's invasion of Russia. It mixes fiction with long reflections on history and is often counted among the greatest novels ever written.

title: The Sistine Chapel Ceiling
body: Michelangelo painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel in the Vatican between 1508 and 1512, including The Creation of Adam. The Last Judgment on the altar wall came later. The work is a high point of the High Renaissance.

title: Hamlet
body: Written around 1600, Hamlet is Shakespeare's longest play. The drama of the Danish prince who hesitates to avenge his father is among the most performed and analysed works in world literature.

title: The Iliad and the Odyssey
body: The two epic poems attributed to Homer date from around the 8th century BC. The Iliad tells of the Trojan War, the Odyssey of Odysseus' long journey home. They are the foundation of Western literature.

title: The Mona Lisa
body: Leonardo da Vinci worked on the portrait from about 1503 and kept it with him for years. Its soft transitions of light and shadow, known as sfumato, are much admired. It hangs in the Louvre and became world-famous partly after being stolen in 1911.

title: Guernica
body: Pablo Picasso painted Guernica in 1937 in response to the bombing of the Basque town during the Spanish Civil War. The huge black, white and grey canvas has become one of the best-known images against war. It hangs in the Museo Reina Sofía in Madrid.

title: Pride and Prejudice
body: Jane Austen's novel of 1813 follows Elizabeth Bennet and Mr Darcy. Its ironic portrait of marriage, money and class in English gentry society made it one of the most widely read novels in English.

title: Gothic Architecture
body: Gothic architecture emerged in France in the 12th century. Pointed arches, ribbed vaults and flying buttresses allowed taller buildings with large stained-glass windows, as in the cathedrals of Chartres and Notre-Dame de Paris.

title: The Night Watch
body: Rembrandt painted this group portrait of an Amsterdam militia company in 1642. Instead of a static row of figures he showed them in motion, with dramatic light. It is among the most famous works of the Dutch Golden Age and hangs in the Rijksmuseum.

title: Franz Kafka
body: In The Metamorphosis (1915) a man wakes up transformed into a giant insect. Kafka's stories of powerless individuals facing absurd systems gave rise to the word Kafkaesque. Much of his work was published after his death by his friend Max Brod, against his wishes.

title: A Doll's House
body: Henrik Ibsen's play of 1879 ends with Nora leaving her husband and children to find herself. The ending caused a scandal, and the play is a landmark of modern realist drama and of debates about women's place in marriage.

title: Cubism
body: Pablo Picasso and Georges Braque developed Cubism around 1907–1914. Instead of a single viewpoint, they broke objects into geometric shapes seen from several angles at once. It was one of the most influential movements in modern art.

title: The Popol Vuh
body: The Popol Vuh is the sacred narrative of the K'iche' Maya of Guatemala, written down in the Latin alphabet in the mid-16th century. It tells of the creation of the world, the adventures of the Hero Twins in the underworld and the history of K'iche' rulers. It survives through a copy made by the friar Francisco Ximénez around 1700 and is the most important work of Maya literature.

title: Romanticism in Art and Literature
body: Romanticism was a movement in art and literature from the late 18th to the mid-19th century that valued emotion, imagination and nature over the reason of the Enlightenment. It includes the poetry of Wordsworth, Byron and Shelley and the paintings of Caspar David Friedrich, Turner and Delacroix. Its fascination with the sublime, the individual and the national past shaped modern culture.

title: Abstract Expressionism
body: Abstract Expressionism arose in New York in the 1940s and 1950s, the first American art movement to gain major influence abroad. Jackson Pollock dripped and poured paint onto canvases laid on the floor, while Mark Rothko painted large, glowing fields of colour. Its success helped shift the centre of the Western art world from Paris to New York.

title: Mimar Sinan
body: Mimar Sinan was chief architect of the Ottoman Empire for about 50 years in the 16th century, serving Suleiman the Magnificent and his successors. He designed hundreds of buildings, including the Süleymaniye Mosque in Istanbul and the Selimiye Mosque in Edirne, which he regarded as his masterpiece. His great domed mosques defined classical Ottoman architecture.

title: Ovid's Metamorphoses
body: Ovid completed his long Latin poem around AD 8, the year the emperor Augustus exiled him to the Black Sea. Linking over 200 myths by the theme of transformation, it retells stories such as Apollo and Daphne, Narcissus, and Pyramus and Thisbe. It became the main source through which later European writers and painters knew classical mythology.

title: Half of a Yellow Sun
body: Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie's novel of 2006 is set during the Nigerian Civil War of 1967 to 1970, when the breakaway state of Biafra fought for independence. Told through characters of different backgrounds, it shows the war's human cost, including famine. It won the Orange Prize for Fiction and brought the war to a new generation of readers.

title: Citizen Kane
body: Orson Welles co-wrote, directed and starred in Citizen Kane, released in 1941 when he was in his mid-twenties. Tracing the life of a newspaper tycoon through the memories of different witnesses, it used deep-focus photography, low camera angles and inventive sound. It is widely regarded as one of the most innovative films ever made.

title: The Shahnameh
body: The Persian poet Ferdowsi completed the Shahnameh, or Book of Kings, around 1010 after some three decades of work. In about 50,000 couplets it tells the history of Iran from mythical times to the Arab conquest, including the deeds of the hero Rostam. Written in a Persian with few Arabic words, it helped preserve the language and is Iran's national epic.

title: Chingiz Aitmatov
body: Chingiz Aitmatov, from Soviet Kyrgyzstan, was the best-known Central Asian writer of the 20th century. His novella Jamilia of 1958, a love story set in a wartime village, was translated into French by the poet Louis Aragon, who praised it highly. Novels such as The Day Lasts More Than a Hundred Years combined Kyrgyz legend with reflection on Soviet life.

title: The Canterbury Tales
body: Geoffrey Chaucer wrote The Canterbury Tales in the late 14th century and left it unfinished at his death in 1400. A group of pilgrims travelling to Canterbury tell each other stories, from the courtly Knight to the bawdy Miller and the Wife of Bath. Written in English rather than French or Latin, it helped establish English as a literary language.

title: The Ramayana
body: The Ramayana, attributed to the sage Valmiki, is a Sanskrit epic about Prince Rama, whose wife Sita is abducted by Ravana, the demon king of Lanka. With the help of the monkey hero Hanuman, Rama rescues her. Retold in many languages and art forms, from Tulsidas's Hindi version to Thai and Javanese dance, it is one of the most influential stories in Asia.

title: Madame Bovary
body: Gustave Flaubert's novel, serialised in 1856 and published as a book in 1857, tells of Emma Bovary, a doctor's wife in provincial Normandy whose romantic dreams lead to adultery, debt and suicide. Flaubert was prosecuted for offending public morals and acquitted. His precise, impersonal style made the book a model of literary realism.

title: Satyajit Ray's Apu Trilogy
body: The Bengali director Satyajit Ray released Pather Panchali in 1955, the first film of a trilogy following Apu from a village childhood to adulthood in Calcutta. Shot on a tiny budget with largely non-professional actors, it brought Indian cinema to international attention. Ray received an honorary Academy Award shortly before his death in 1992.

title: The Bust of Nefertiti
body: This painted limestone bust of Queen Nefertiti, wife of the pharaoh Akhenaten, was made in the 14th century BC and found in 1912 in the workshop of the sculptor Thutmose at Amarna. With its elegant long neck and tall crown, it is one of the most famous images from ancient Egypt. It is kept in Berlin, and Egypt has long called for its return.

title: Bernini
body: Gian Lorenzo Bernini was the leading sculptor and architect of Baroque Rome in the 17th century. Marble works such as Apollo and Daphne and The Ecstasy of Saint Teresa capture moments of intense movement and emotion. He also designed the colonnade of St Peter's Square, which embraces visitors like a pair of arms.

title: The Epic of Sundiata
body: The Epic of Sundiata tells of the founder of the Mali Empire in the 13th century, a boy unable to walk who grows into a hero and defeats the sorcerer-king Sumanguru. It has been passed down orally for centuries by griots, the hereditary bards of West Africa who are also historians and genealogists. It is one of the great epics of African oral literature.

title: The Parthenon
body: The Parthenon was built on the Acropolis of Athens between 447 and 432 BC as a temple to the goddess Athena. Designed by Ictinus and Callicrates, with sculpture overseen by Phidias, it is the supreme example of the Doric order. Many of its surviving sculptures, the Elgin Marbles, are in the British Museum, and Greece has long sought their return.

title: Wole Soyinka
body: The Nigerian playwright and poet Wole Soyinka became the first Black African to receive the Nobel Prize in Literature, in 1986. Plays such as Death and the King's Horseman blend Yoruba myth and ritual with European dramatic forms. He was imprisoned during the Nigerian Civil War and became an outspoken critic of military dictatorship.

title: The Moai of Rapa Nui
body: The people of Rapa Nui, or Easter Island, carved nearly a thousand monumental stone figures known as moai, most of them between roughly the 13th and 16th centuries. Thought to represent deified ancestors, many stood on stone platforms facing inland, watching over the communities. How they were moved is debated, though many researchers think they were 'walked' upright with ropes.
